questions.stem: An ionic compound such as potassium oxide contains K+ and O2- ions. What overall charge does the compound carry?

options.text: No overall charge, because the two 1+ charges cancel the single 2- charge
options.explanation: The compound is neutral because two potassium ions supply exactly the two positive charges that one oxide ion balances.

options.text: A 1- charge, because oxide has the larger charge
options.explanation: The compound as a whole cannot inherit one ion's leftover charge; the ion counts adjust until the charges cancel.
options.misconception: ion charge carried through to the whole compound

options.text: A 1+ charge, because there are two potassium ions
options.explanation: Counting ions instead of comparing charge sizes misreads the balance; the two 1+ charges together cancel the 2-.
options.misconception: ion count mistaken for net charge

options.text: It depends on the size of the crystals
options.explanation: Neutrality is fixed by the ion charges and their ratio, not by how much compound is present.
options.misconception: macroscopic quantity thought to affect charge balance

questions.stem: Using direct comparison, what is the formula of calcium chloride, formed from Ca2+ and Cl- ions?

options.text: CaCl2
options.explanation: The single 2+ charge needs two 1- chloride ions to cancel, so the formula carries two chlorides.

options.text: CaCl
options.explanation: Matching one of each ion leaves a net 1+ charge, so the compound would not be neutral.
options.misconception: one-of-each assumption ignoring unequal charges

options.text: Ca2Cl
options.explanation: Doubling the calcium gives a net 2+ and leaves the charges even further from cancelling.
options.misconception: counts swapped between the ions

options.text: Ca2Cl2
options.explanation: Although these counts do cancel the charges, the formula must be given as the simplest whole-number ratio, which is CaCl2.
options.misconception: unsimplified ratio accepted

questions.stem: The sulfate ion carries a 2- charge. Why does iron(II) sulfate need no brackets in its formula?

options.text: Because only one sulfate ion pairs with each iron(II) ion
options.explanation: Brackets are needed only when more than one of a complex ion appears; the one-to-one match here makes brackets unnecessary.

options.text: Because sulfate is a simple ion, not a complex one
options.explanation: Sulfate is a complex ion with several atoms; it is its count of one, not its structure, that removes the need for brackets.
options.misconception: complex-ion structure confused with the bracket rule

options.text: Because iron and sulfate carry opposite charges
options.explanation: Opposite charges are true of every ionic compound and never by themselves decide whether brackets appear.
options.misconception: charge difference read as the bracket trigger

options.text: Because the metal is always written first in the formula
options.explanation: Element order governs writing order, not bracket use; brackets track multi-ion counts.
options.misconception: ordering rule misapplied to brackets

questions.stem: A student writes the formula of sodium oxide, formed from Na+ and O2-, as NaO. What is wrong with this?

options.text: The charges do not cancel: two sodium ions are needed for each oxide ion, so the formula is Na2O
options.explanation: One 1+ charge cannot balance one 2- charge; the direct comparison shows the 2- remains, so the sodium count must double.

options.text: Nothing: one of each ion is always the correct ratio
options.explanation: A one-of-each ratio only works when the charges are equal and opposite; here a 1- charge would remain.
options.misconception: one-of-each rule overgeneralised

options.text: The metal should be written second, giving ONa
options.explanation: Convention writes the metal first, but reordering the symbols would not fix the unbalanced charge.
options.misconception: cosmetic rule treated as the error

options.text: Sodium oxide is covalent, so ionic formula rules do not apply
options.explanation: Sodium oxide is ionic, formed between a metal and a non-metal, so the charge-cancellation method applies fully.
options.misconception: bonding type misclassified

questions.stem: Why must an ionic formula describe a ratio of ions rather than a single molecule?

options.text: Because the lattice repeats the ion pattern throughout, so the formula gives the simplest repeating ratio
options.explanation: The giant lattice continues in every direction, and the formula states the fixed ratio of ions within that repeating structure.

options.text: Because ions are too small to count individually
options.explanation: The ratio form reflects the structure of the lattice, not the difficulty of counting particles.
options.misconception: size-based reasoning about formula style

options.text: Because ionic compounds always contain exactly two types of ion
options.explanation: Some ionic compounds contain more than two ion types; the ratio form exists because of the lattice, not the variety of ions.
options.misconception: ion variety mistaken for the reason

options.text: Because the charges would double if a molecule were written
options.explanation: Charge balance is unchanged by how the formula is written; the ratio form reflects the repeating lattice.
options.misconception: formula style thought to alter charges

questions.stem: State the overall charge of every ionic compound, and how the ion charges relate to produce it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ionic compounds carry no overall charge: the positive and negative charges on their ions cancel exactly.

questions.stem: State the formula of iron(II) sulfate, given that the sulfate ion carries a 2- charge and the iron(II) ion a 2+ charge.
questions.modelAnswer: One sulfate ion, carrying 2-, exactly cancels the 2+ charge on the iron(II) ion, so the formula is FeSO4.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between saying an ionic compound is neutral and saying an atom is neutral.
questions.modelAnswer: The neutrality belongs to the compound as a whole: its positive and negative ion charges cancel exactly, whereas a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons in one single particle — the two statements are not the same.

questions.stem: Aluminium oxide is built from Al3+ ions and O2- ions. Using the direct comparison method of record, work out the formula and justify the ion counts.
questions.modelAnswer: The charges are not equal in size, so more than one of each ion is needed: 2 x 3+ = 6+ from two aluminium ions cancels 3 x 2- = 6- from three oxide ions, giving the formula Al2O3.

questions.stem: Aluminium oxide forms from Al3+ and O2- ions. Which formula do the swapped counts give?

options.text: Al2O3
options.explanation: The 3 on aluminium becomes the count of oxide ions, and the 2 on oxide becomes the count of aluminium ions, giving Al2O3.

options.text: Al3O2
options.explanation: Dropping each number onto its own ion skips the swap; the 3 belongs to the oxide count.
options.misconception: counts dropped straight down without swapping

options.text: AlO
options.explanation: Treating the charges as equal assumes one of each cancels, but a net 1+ charge would remain.
options.misconception: unequal charges assumed equal

options.text: Al3O3
options.explanation: Copying the 3 onto both ions ignores the 2 on oxide; the counts exchange rather than repeat.
options.misconception: count copied instead of swapped

questions.stem: A student applies swap-and-drop to calcium sulfide, from Ca2+ and S2-, and writes Ca2S2. What correction is required?

options.text: Reduce the ratio to its simplest whole numbers, giving CaS
options.explanation: Equal charges cancel one-to-one, so the dropped counts both divide by two and the formula is CaS.

options.text: Keep Ca2S2, since it shows both charges
options.explanation: The formula must state the simplest ratio; Ca2S2 carries the same ratio twice over.
options.misconception: explicit counts preferred over simplest form

options.text: Swap again to give S2Ca2
options.explanation: A second swap only reorders the same unsimplified counts and still needs reducing.
options.misconception: method reapplied instead of simplifying

options.text: Change the charges to 1+ and 1- before swapping
options.explanation: The ions genuinely carry 2+ and 2-; it is the written counts, not the charges, that get reduced.
options.misconception: charges edited to fit the answer

questions.stem: Calcium hydroxide forms from Ca2+ and OH- ions. Which formula is correct?

options.text: Ca(OH)2
options.explanation: The 2+ calcium needs two hydroxide ions, and the whole OH group is bracketed before the 2 is applied.

options.text: CaOH2
options.explanation: Without brackets the 2 appears to multiply only the hydrogen, distorting the group count.
options.misconception: brackets omitted around a doubled complex ion

options.text: Ca2OH
options.explanation: The counts have been swapped the wrong way; calcium's 2 belongs to the hydroxide count.
options.misconception: swap direction reversed

options.text: CaOH
options.explanation: One hydroxide ion cancels only one of calcium's two positive charges, leaving a net 1+.
options.misconception: unequal charges treated as equal

questions.stem: Which pair of steps correctly builds the formula of copper(II) chloride?

options.text: Identify Cu2+ and Cl-, then swap so two chloride ions pair with one copper ion, giving CuCl2
options.explanation: The copper ion's 2 sets the chloride count, and the chloride ion's 1 sets the copper count, which is never written.

options.text: Identify Cu2+ and Cl-, then give each ion a count of 1, giving CuCl
options.explanation: Equal counts leave the 2+ uncancelled; the charge numbers must cross over between the ions.
options.misconception: uniform count applied to both ions

options.text: Combine the charge numbers into 3 and attach it to copper, giving Cu3Cl
options.explanation: The magnitudes swap rather than combine; the 2 and the 1 become each other's ion counts.
options.misconception: charges merged instead of swapped

options.text: Write CuCl2 because chloride always doubles
options.explanation: The two chlorides follow from copper's 2+ charge, not from a fixed rule about chlorine.
options.misconception: element habit substituted for the method

questions.stem: Iron wool burns in chlorine to form a compound containing Fe3+ and Cl- ions. Which name and formula result?

options.text: Iron chloride, FeCl3
options.explanation: Three 1- chloride ions cancel the 3+ charge, and the metal keeps its name while chlorine becomes chloride.

options.text: Iron(III) chlorine, FeCl3
options.explanation: The non-metal takes the -ide ending in an ionic name; chlorine as a name fragment is reserved for the element itself.
options.misconception: naming rule misapplied to the non-metal

options.text: Iron chloride, FeCl
options.explanation: One chloride leaves two of iron's three charges uncancelled; the counts must come from the charge sizes.
options.misconception: one-of-each ratio reused

options.text: Iron trichloride, Fe3Cl
options.explanation: Prefix naming is not used for ionic compounds, and the counts sit on the wrong ions.
options.misconception: covalent naming transferred to ionic compounds

questions.stem: Describe the swap-and-drop rule for building an ionic formula from two ion charges.
questions.modelAnswer: Swap-and-drop turns each ion's charge number into the other ion's count: as Cu2+ with Cl- gives CuCl2.

questions.stem: State what is done with the positive and negative signs during swap-and-drop, and how a count of 1 is handled.
questions.modelAnswer: Positive and negative signs are dropped during the method, and a count of 1 is never written.

questions.stem: Explain why applying swap-and-drop to Ca2+ and S2- must not stop at Ca2S2, and what the correct formula is.
questions.modelAnswer: With same-charge ions the method overcounts, so the resulting ratio must be reduced to its simplest whole numbers; Ca2S2 reduces to CaS, the correct formula of calcium sulfide.

questions.stem: Magnesium hydroxide forms from Mg2+ ions and OH- ions. Apply swap-and-drop, and explain why brackets appear in the final formula.
questions.modelAnswer: The 2+ charge swaps to give two hydroxide groups, and because the whole OH- group is doubled the formula is written Mg(OH)2 with the group inside brackets.
